questions.question: A spinner has 4 equal parts. One part is red, one is blue, one is green and one is yellow. Sofia spins the arrow once. How many different outcomes are possible for that one spin?
options: 4, one for each colour the arrow could stop on
2, because it either lands on your colour or it does not
1, because the arrow stops on only one part
16, because 4 times 4 is 16
questions.explain: The possible outcomes are all the different results one spin could give: red, blue, green or yellow, so there are 4. The common trap is thinking about what actually happens on the spin (one result) instead of everything that could happen.

questions.question: A spinner has 6 equal parts numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Parts 2 and 5 are shaded blue and the other 4 parts are white. Ravi spins once and writes down the number the arrow lands on. Which list shows all the possible outcomes?
options: 2 and 5
questions.explain: Ravi is recording the number, so every numbered part is a possible outcome: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The common trap is letting the shading take over and listing only the shaded numbers or only the white ones.

questions.question: A spinner has 5 equal parts. Three parts are labelled ‘cat’ and two parts are labelled ‘dog’. Mia spins the arrow once and reads the word it lands on. How many different possible outcomes are there for the word?
questions.explain: Only two different words can be read, cat or dog, so there are 2 possible outcomes even though there are 5 parts. The common trap is counting parts instead of counting the different results, since repeated labels give the same outcome.

questions.question: A spinner has 8 equal parts. Four parts are red, three parts are green and one part is white. Noah spins the arrow once. Which list shows all the different colours the arrow could land on?
options: red
red and green
red, red, red, red, green, green, green, white
red, green and white
questions.explain: List each different colour once: red, green, white. The common trap is dropping white because only one part has it — a colour with just one part is still a possible outcome.

questions.question: A bag holds four tiles marked 3, 5, 5 and 8. One tile is drawn without looking. How many different possible outcomes are there for the number drawn?
questions.explain: The different numbers that can be drawn are 3, 5 and 8, so there are 3 possible outcomes. The common trap is counting the tiles (4) instead of the different results, because the two tiles marked 5 give the same outcome.

questions.question: A number cube has faces numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. It is rolled once. Which of these is NOT a possible outcome of that roll?
questions.explain: A possible outcome has to be something written on the cube, and there is no 0 face, so 0 cannot happen. The common trap is thinking any small number is fine — an outcome must come from the list of results the object can actually give.

questions.question: One item is drawn without looking. Which bag gives exactly 4 different possible outcomes for one draw?
options: a bag with 2 red tiles and 2 blue tiles
a bag with 4 red tiles
a bag with tiles marked 2, 4, 6 and 8
a bag with tiles marked 7, 7, 7 and 9
questions.explain: Count the different results, not the items: 2, 4, 6, 8 gives four different outcomes. The common trap is picking a bag just because it holds 4 items — 4 red tiles give only one possible outcome, red.

questions.question: Which of these single events has exactly 2 possible outcomes?
options: rolling a number cube numbered 1 to 6 once
drawing one tile from a bag with tiles marked 1, 2, 3 and 4
spinning a spinner with 3 equal parts: red, blue and green
flipping a coin once
questions.explain: A coin flip can only give heads or tails, so it has 2 possible outcomes. The common trap is thinking every event has two outcomes — the number of outcomes always comes from the make-up of the object you are using.

questions.question: At a school fair in Surrey, a prize spinner has 10 equal parts. Nine parts say ‘small prize’ and one part says ‘big prize’. Jason says, ‘There is really only one possible outcome, small prize, because it almost always lands there.’ Which statement is correct?
options: There are 2 possible outcomes, small prize and big prize; big prize is unlikely but still possible.
There are 10 possible outcomes, one for each equal part, because each part the pointer can stop on counts.
There is only 1 possible outcome, because 9 of the 10 parts say small prize and that is nearly the whole spinner.
Jason is right — big prize is impossible, because the spinner almost never lands on it, so it does not count.
questions.explain: Listing outcomes means listing every result that could happen, so small prize and big prize both belong on the list. The common trap is mixing up ‘unlikely’ with ‘impossible’ — a result with only one part is still a possible outcome.

questions.question: Priya picks her after-school activity by drawing one card from a bag. The bag holds 6 cards: swim, swim, skate, bike, bike, bike. In December her family adds one new card that says ski. Priya then draws one card. How many different possible outcomes does she have now?
questions.explain: First list the different activities in the bag — swim, skate, bike — then add the new one, giving swim, skate, bike, ski, which is 4 possible outcomes. The common trap is counting all 7 cards, but the three bike cards all lead to the same outcome.

questions.question: Liam has 6 coins loose in his jacket pocket: three $1 coins, two $2 coins and one quarter ($0.25). He gives the quarter to his sister for the bottle return, then pulls out one coin from the pocket without looking. How many different possible outcomes are there for the amount he pulls out?
questions.explain: After the quarter is gone, only $1 and $2 coins are left, so the different amounts he could pull out are $1 or $2 — 2 possible outcomes. The common trap is forgetting the quarter was removed, or counting the 5 coins left instead of the different amounts.

questions.question: Nina's spinner has 3 equal parts: red, blue and green. She spins it and gets red, then spins again and gets red a second time. She is about to spin a third time. Which statement about the possible outcomes of the third spin is correct?
options: Only blue or green, because red has already come up twice, so red has used up its turns
Only red, because the spinner is landing on red today, so it will keep landing there
Red, blue or green, but red is not allowed to come up three times in a row on a fair spinner
Red, blue or green — each spin is an independent event, so all three are still possible
questions.explain: Each spin is an independent event: the spinner does not remember earlier spins, so the possible outcomes are still red, blue and green. The common trap is thinking a colour gets ‘used up’ or is ‘due’ — past results never change the list of possible outcomes.
